title: 22. Interview: Apache Kafka
summary: Interview Q&A for Apache Kafka — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Apache Kafka interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is Kafka called a "log" rather than a "queue," and what does that distinction imply?
**Answer:** A queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) removes a message after a consumer acks — the message has a single lifecycle from producer to one consumer. A log (Kafka) retains messages for a configurable period (days to weeks) and lets multiple independent consumers read the same message at different times, replay it from the beginning, or skip ahead. The log abstraction has three implications. First, **multi-consumer fan-out**: multiple consumer groups read the same topic independently — Netflix's playback events are read by real-time recommendations (sub-second lag), batch analytics (hours lag), and billing (minutes lag), all from one topic, with no producer changes. Second, **replay**: a new consumer can read from offset 0 and rebuild its view of the world — when LinkedIn adds a new fraud-detection service, it reads the last 7 days of events and catches up, without backfilling from a separate store. Third, **offset-based delivery**: consumers track their position by committing offsets, not by acking individual messages — this is more efficient (batch commit) but requires idempotent consumers because redelivery happens on crash (at-least-once). The architect's rule: Kafka is the right choice when multi-consumer fan-out, replay, or high throughput is required; a queue is the right choice when point-to-point delivery with per-message ack is required.
**Visual:**
```
queue:  produce -> deliver to ONE consumer -> ack -> REMOVE (single lifecycle)
log:    produce -> retain N days -> many consumer groups read at own pace
        Netflix: 1 topic -> recommendations (1s lag) + analytics (1h lag) + billing (1m lag)
replay: new consumer reads from offset 0 -> catches up without backfill
offset-based delivery (not per-msg ack) -> batch commit, idempotent consumer needed
```

### Q2. How does partitioning work, and why is the partition count the parallelism ceiling?
**Answer:** A Kafka topic is split into N partitions, each an ordered append-only log. The producer chooses a partition by hashing the message key (key=null means round-robin), so all messages with the same key land in the same partition in order — this is how Kafka guarantees per-key ordering. Within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so a topic with N partitions supports at most N consumers in a group (extra consumers are idle). This makes the partition count the parallelism ceiling: a topic with 12 partitions can be consumed by at most 12 parallel consumers, regardless of how many messages are backlogged. The operational implication is critical: if you under-provision partitions (e.g., 3 partitions for a topic that needs 12 consumers), you cap throughput and cannot fix it without re-partitioning, which breaks key-based ordering (a key hashed to partition 5 may hash to partition 17 after a re-partition, splitting its history). The rule is to over-provision partitions from the start (12–24 for a high-throughput topic, even if you need only 3 today) to avoid re-partitioning. LinkedIn's `user_events` topic has 1000 partitions to support 1000 parallel consumers; Uber's `trip_events` has 256. The architect's rule: choose partition count = max(expected consumers, throughput / 10MB-per-partition-sec), and never decrease partitions.
**Visual:**
```
topic: 3 partitions, key hashing:
  key=user_1 -> hash -> partition 0 -> [msg0, msg1, ...] (per-key order preserved)
  key=user_2 -> hash -> partition 1 -> [msg0, ...]
  key=user_3 -> hash -> partition 2 -> [msg0, ...]
consumer group with 3 consumers -> each gets 1 partition (3-way parallel)
  add a 4th consumer -> IDLE (only 3 partitions)
  fix: increase partitions, but breaks key->partition mapping (re-partition risk)
rule: partition count = parallelism ceiling; over-provision from day 1
```

### Q3. What is the ISR (In-Sync Replicas), and how does it interact with the producer's `acks` setting?
**Answer:** Each partition has one leader replica and N follower replicas (replication factor, typically 3). The leader handles all reads and writes; followers replicate by fetching from the leader. The **ISR** is the set of replicas that are fully caught up with the leader (within a configurable lag, default 10 seconds). If a follower falls behind, it is removed from the ISR; if it catches up, it is added back. The producer's `acks` setting determines durability. `acks=0` (fire-and-forget): the producer sends and does not wait for any ack — fastest, but the message may be lost on broker crash. `acks=1` (leader-only): the leader writes to its log and acks; if the leader crashes before followers replicate, the message is lost. `acks=all` (default in modern Kafka): the leader waits for all ISR replicas to acknowledge before acking the producer — the message is durable as long as at least one ISR replica survives. The trade-off is latency: `acks=all` adds the replication round-trip (typically 5–20ms) but guarantees durability. The architect's rule: use `acks=all` with `min.insync.replicas=2` and `replication.factor=3` for any data that matters — this tolerates one broker failure without data loss. `acks=1` is acceptable for ephemeral telemetry; `acks=0` is almost never right. Netflix and Uber use `acks=all` for all production topics, accepting the latency for durability.
**Visual:**
```
partition with RF=3: leader L, followers F1, F2. ISR = {L, F1, F2} if all caught up.
acks=0:  produce -> send -> done (no wait) -> lost on leader crash
acks=1:  produce -> leader writes -> ack (followers may lag) -> lost if leader crashes
acks=all: produce -> leader writes -> ALL ISR ack -> ack producer -> durable if 1 ISR survives
config: acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 + RF=3 -> tolerate 1 broker failure, no loss
```

### Q4. How do consumer groups and rebalances work, and why are rebalances an operational pain point?
**Answer:** A consumer group is a set of consumers that share a topic: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, so the group reads the topic in parallel. Different consumer groups read independently — each tracks its own offsets. A **rebalance** occurs when consumers join or leave the group (scale up, crash, deploy): Kafka reassigns partitions to the new set of consumers. During a rebalance, consumption pauses — all consumers stop reading while the new assignment is computed and communicated, causing a brief stall (seconds to minutes for large groups). The pain points: (1) **stop-the-world**: the default rebalance protocol (eager) pauses all consumers, even those whose partitions did not change; (2) **cascading rebalances**: if one consumer is slow to respond (e.g., long GC), the coordinator assumes it is dead and triggers a rebalance, which triggers more rebalances; (3) **offset commits**: a consumer must commit its offset before the rebalance or risk redelivery of in-flight messages. The mitigations: **incremental cooperative rebalancing** (KIP-429, default in modern Kafka) only revokes partitions that need to move, avoiding stop-the-world; **static partition assignment** (KIP-429) keeps assignments stable across restarts; **session timeout** tuning (`session.timeout.ms=30s`, `heartbeat.interval.ms=3s`) prevents false-positive dead detections. The architect's rule: tune the rebalance protocol for your workload — cooperative rebalancing for large groups (>20 consumers), static assignment for stateful consumers (stream processing with local state), and monitor rebalance frequency (more than 1/hour indicates instability).
**Visual:**
```
group of 3 consumers, 6 partitions (2 each): c1={P0,P1}, c2={P2,P3}, c3={P4,P5}
c2 crashes -> rebalance -> c1={P0,P1,P2}, c3={P3,P4,P5} (consumption pauses)
pain: stop-the-world (eager), cascading (slow GC -> false death -> more rebalances)
mitigations:
  cooperative rebalancing (KIP-429): only move changed partitions, no stop-the-world
  static assignment: stable across restarts
  session.timeout.ms=30s, heartbeat=3s -> avoid false positives
```

### Q5. How does Kafka achieve exactly-once delivery, and when should you use it?
**Answer:** Kafka's default is at-least-once: producers retry on failure (may duplicate), and consumers crash and redeliver (may duplicate). Exactly-once (EOS) is supported via the **transactional producer** and **read-processed** semantics. The transactional producer sets a `transactional.id` and uses a two-phase commit: (1) `beginTransaction`, (2) produce messages to one or more input topics and write to one or more output topics, (3) `commitTransaction` (atomically writes all output messages and the consumer's offset commit). Consumers set `isolation.level=read_committed` to see only committed transactions. The result: a stream-processing app (Kafka Streams, Flink) reads from input, processes, writes to output, and commits its input offset atomically — if it crashes mid-transaction, the entire transaction is rolled back, and on restart it re-reads from the last committed offset, processing the input exactly once. The trade-off is overhead: EOS adds 10–20% latency (transaction coordination) and reduces throughput (batching is constrained by transaction boundaries). The architect's rule: use EOS for financial transactions (debits, credits, transfers) where duplicates are unacceptable; use at-least-once with idempotent consumers for everything else. Most Kafka deployments are at-least-once because the idempotent-consumer pattern (use a `message_id` and dedup on the consumer side) is simpler and faster than EOS. Square and Stripe use EOS for their payment pipelines; Netflix and Uber use at-least-once with idempotent consumers for most pipelines.
**Visual:**
```
at-least-once (default): produce retry -> may dup; consumer crash -> may dup
  fix: idempotent consumer (message_id dedup)
exactly-once (EOS): transactional.id + 2PC
  beginTxn -> produce to output topics + commit input offset -> commitTxn (atomic)
  consumer: isolation.level=read_committed -> sees only committed txns
  crash mid-txn -> rollback -> restart re-reads from last committed offset
trade-off: 10-20% latency, lower throughput
use EOS: financial (debits, credits); use at-least-once: everything else
```

### Q6. How does Kafka's retention work, and how do you choose between time-based and size-based retention?
**Answer:** Kafka retains messages on disk until they are deleted by retention policy. **Time-based retention** (`retention.ms`, default 7 days) deletes segments older than the threshold — simple, predictable, and the default for most topics. **Size-based retention** (`retention.bytes`, default -1 = unlimited) deletes the oldest segments when the partition exceeds the size limit — useful when disk space is the constraint, not time. **Log compaction** (`cleanup.policy=compact`) is a third mode: instead of deleting by time or size, Kafka keeps only the latest message for each key — turning the topic into a key-value store where the value is the latest state. Compaction is used for changelog topics (e.g., a `user_profile` topic where each update overwrites the previous state for that user_id) and for Kafka Streams' state stores. The choice depends on the use case: time-based for event streams where historical replay matters (7–30 days for operational debugging, longer for analytics); size-based for high-volume topics where disk is the constraint; compaction for state snapshots where only the latest per key matters. The architect's rule: default to `retention.ms=7d` for most topics; increase to 30d for topics that feed analytics (replay value); use compaction for state-changelog topics (e.g., `user_profile_changes` where the latest is the current state). LinkedIn's `user_events` topic has 7-day retention (operational); the analytics warehouse has 30-day retention (replay for backfill); the `user_profile` changelog is compacted (KV store).
**Visual:**
```
retention.ms=7d (default): delete segments older than 7 days -> replay last week
retention.bytes=10GB: delete oldest when partition exceeds 10GB -> disk-bounded
log compaction: keep only latest per key -> KV store (user_profile_changes)
choose:
  event stream (debug replay): 7d time-based
  analytics (backfill):        30d time-based
  state changelog (KV):        compacted (latest per key)
LinkedIn: user_events=7d, analytics=30d, user_profile=compacted
```

### Q7. What is consumer lag, and why is it the single most important Kafka operational metric?
**Answer:** Consumer lag is the difference between the latest offset in a partition and the consumer's committed offset — it measures how far behind the consumer is. Lag = 0 means the consumer is caught up; lag = 10000 means the consumer has 10000 unprocessed messages. Lag is the single most important metric because it directly reflects whether the consumer can keep up with the producer: if lag is stable (even if non-zero), the consumer is keeping up; if lag is growing, the consumer is overwhelmed and will eventually fail SLAs. The causes of growing lag: (1) **consumer too slow** (CPU-bound processing, slow downstream DB writes) — fix by adding consumers (if partitions allow) or optimizing processing; (2) **too few partitions** (cannot add consumers because all partitions are assigned) — fix by re-partitioning (painful) or scaling vertically; (3) **consumer crashes/rebalances** (frequent rebalances pause consumption) — fix by tuning rebalance settings; (4) **producer spikes** (a burst of traffic overwhelms a normally-adequate consumer) — fix by autoscaling consumers or buffering. The alerting pattern: alert on `lag > threshold` (e.g., 10000 messages) AND on `lag growing over 5 minutes` (the trend matters more than the absolute value). Tools like Burrow (LinkedIn's lag monitor), Confluent Control Center, and Datadog's Kafka integration provide lag metrics per consumer group and partition. The architect's rule: instrument lag from day one, alert on it, and have a runbook for "lag is growing" that includes scaling consumers, checking for rebalances, and inspecting the consumer's processing time.
**Visual:**
```
lag = latest_offset - committed_offset (per partition, per consumer group)
lag=0: caught up; lag=10k: 10k unprocessed msgs; lag growing: consumer overwhelmed
causes:
  1. consumer too slow (CPU, slow DB) -> add consumers (if partitions allow)
  2. too few partitions (cannot add consumers) -> re-partition (painful) or scale up
  3. frequent rebalances (pause consumption) -> tune rebalance settings
  4. producer spike -> autoscale consumers or buffer
alert: lag > 10k OR lag growing over 5 min (trend > absolute)
tools: Burrow, Confluent CC, Datadog
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. LinkedIn's `user_events` topic handles 7 trillion messages per day. How would you size the Kafka cluster to sustain this throughput?
**Answer:** 7 trillion/day = ~81 million messages/sec sustained (peak likely 2–3x = 200M/sec). Sizing is per-broker throughput and per-partition throughput. Per-broker: a well-tuned Kafka broker sustains 100k–1M msgs/sec (depending on message size, batching, and disk). With 1KB messages and 16KB batches, expect ~150k msgs/sec per broker; to sustain 200M/sec, you need ~1300 brokers — but LinkedIn uses compression (Snappy, 3–5x), larger batches (1MB), and faster hardware (NVMe), reaching ~500k msgs/sec per broker, so ~400 brokers. Per-partition: each partition sustains ~10MB/sec; with 1KB messages, that's ~10k msgs/sec per partition; to sustain 200M/sec, you need ~20000 partitions across the topic, spread across 400 brokers (50 partitions per broker). The operational implications: (1) **partition count** must be set at topic creation (20000 partitions for `user_events`), and cannot be reduced later; (2) **consumer parallelism** is capped at partition count, so the analytics pipeline needs up to 20000 consumers; (3) **storage**: 7T msgs/day * 1KB = 7PB/day raw, compressed to ~2PB/day, retained for 7 days = 14PB — distributed across 400 brokers = 35TB per broker, which is feasible with NVMe arrays. LinkedIn's actual cluster has ~1500 brokers across multiple datacenters with cross-cluster replication (MirrorMaker), processing 7T msgs/day with sub-minute consumer lag. The architect's rule: size for peak * 2, over-provision partitions (cannot reduce), and plan storage for retention * compressed throughput.
**Visual:**
```
7T/day = 81M/sec sustained, peak ~200M/sec
per-broker: ~500k msgs/sec (1KB msg, 1MB batch, NVMe, Snappy) -> ~400 brokers
per-partition: ~10k msgs/sec -> need ~20000 partitions (50 per broker)
storage: 7PB/day raw -> ~2PB/day compressed -> 7d retention = 14PB -> 35TB/broker
LinkedIn actual: ~1500 brokers, multi-DC, MirrorMaker, sub-minute lag
rule: size peak*2, over-provision partitions, plan storage = retention * compressed tput
```

### Q2. Netflix's playback pipeline has 3 consumer groups reading the same `playback_events` topic: recommendations (sub-second lag SLA), billing (minutes lag SLA), and analytics (hours lag SLA). How do you isolate them so a slow analytics group does not affect recommendations?
**Answer:** The good news is that Kafka's consumer-group design already isolates them: each group reads independently at its own pace, with its own offsets, and a slow group does not slow down other groups (the broker serves reads from the page cache, and one group's lag does not affect another's reads). The remaining concern is broker load: if the analytics group does a full replay (read from offset 0), it generates heavy read I/O on the brokers, which could affect the recommendations group's fetch latency. The mitigations. First, **separate clusters for different SLAs**: run a low-latency cluster for recommendations and a separate cluster for analytics, with MirrorMaker replicating from the former to the latter. This fully isolates the SLAs — analytics replay does not touch the recommendations cluster. Second, **throttle replay**: if a single cluster is used, throttle the analytics group's fetch rate during replay (Kafka supports per-consumer-group quotas via `kafka-configs.sh`), limiting it to e.g., 50MB/sec so it does not saturate broker I/O. Third, **use follower fetching**: consumers in the analytics group fetch from follower replicas (KIP-392), distributing read load across brokers instead of concentrating on leaders. Fourth, **monitor lag per group**: alert on recommendations lag > 1s (immediate action) and analytics lag > 6h (next-day action) — different SLAs, different alerting. Netflix uses a hybrid: the recommendations cluster is separate (sub-second SLA, dedicated hardware), while billing and analytics share a second cluster (minutes/hours SLA, replicated from the first via MirrorMaker).
**Visual:**
```
Kafka design: each consumer group reads independently -> slow group does not affect others
concern: analytics replay generates heavy read I/O -> affects recommendations fetch latency
fix 1: separate clusters (recs cluster + analytics cluster, MirrorMaker replicate)
fix 2: throttle analytics replay (per-group quotas, 50MB/sec cap)
fix 3: follower fetching (KIP-392) -> distribute read load across brokers
fix 4: per-group lag alerts (recs > 1s = page, analytics > 6h = email)
Netflix: recs cluster (dedicated) + billing/analytics cluster (replicated)
```

### Q3. Uber's `trip_events` topic uses `trip_id` as the key for per-trip ordering, with 256 partitions. A trip's events are split across two partitions after a re-partition to 512. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** The diagnosis is that Kafka's partition assignment is based on `hash(key) % n_partitions`, and changing `n_partitions` changes the partition for most keys — a trip_id that hashed to partition 5 with 256 partitions may hash to partition 17 with 512 partitions, splitting its event history across two partitions and breaking per-trip ordering. This is the fundamental reason Kafka documentation says "you cannot reduce partitions, and increasing them breaks key ordering." The fixes, in order of practicality. First, **avoid re-partitioning** by over-provisioning from the start: if you might need 512 partitions, create 512 from day one, even if you only have 50 consumers today (the extra partitions are idle but cost nothing). This is the recommended pattern. Second, **create a new topic with 512 partitions and migrate**: produce new trips to the new topic, and let consumers transition; old trips continue on the old topic until retention expires. This is clean but operationally complex — all consumers must handle both topics during the migration window. Third, **accept the split and handle it in the consumer**: if the split is unavoidable, the consumer must buffer events per trip_id across both partitions and reorder by sequence number — essentially building application-level ordering on top of Kafka's partition ordering. This is complex and fragile. The architect's rule: partition count is a one-way decision — over-provision at creation (256 or 512 for a high-throughput topic), never re-partition in place, and if you must scale beyond the original count, create a new topic and migrate. Uber learned this the hard way in 2018 and now defaults to 512 partitions for high-throughput topics.
**Visual:**
```
trip_id=T1, 256 partitions: hash(T1) % 256 = 5 -> all T1 events on P5 (ordered)
re-partition to 512:        hash(T1) % 512 = 17 -> new T1 events on P17 (SPLIT)
  -> per-trip ordering broken (P5 has old events, P17 has new)
fix 1 (best): over-provision at creation (512 from day 1, even if 50 consumers)
fix 2: new topic with 512 partitions, migrate (produce new trips to new topic)
fix 3 (worst): consumer buffers per trip_id across partitions, reorder by seq
rule: partition count is one-way; over-provision, never re-partition in place
```

### Q4. A Kafka topic has 12 partitions and a consumer group with 12 consumers. After a deploy, one consumer is slow to start (long JVM warmup), triggering a rebalance that pauses all 12 consumers for 30 seconds. How do you prevent this?
**Answer:** The diagnosis is the eager rebalance protocol: when a consumer joins, the coordinator pauses all consumers, computes the new assignment, and resumes — the slow-starting consumer's join triggers a stop-the-world for the entire group. The fixes, in order of impact. First, **incremental cooperative rebalancing** (KIP-429, default in Kafka 2.4+): instead of revoking all partitions and reassigning, the protocol only revokes partitions that need to move, and the join of a new consumer does not pause existing consumers until the new consumer is ready to receive partitions. This eliminates stop-the-world for joins. Second, **static partition assignment** (KIP-429 `partition.assignment.strategy=StickyAssignor` or `CooperativeStickyAssignor`): the assignment is stable across restarts, so a restarting consumer gets its old partitions back without reassignment of other consumers. Third, **rolling deploys with `cooperative-sticky`**: deploy one consumer at a time; each restart triggers a small rebalance that only affects the restarting consumer's partitions, not the whole group. Fourth, **warm up before joining**: the consumer initializes its JVM, loads caches, and connects to downstream dependencies BEFORE joining the group — once it joins, it is immediately ready to consume, reducing the rebalance window. Fifth, **tune `session.timeout.ms` and `heartbeat.interval.ms`**: set `session.timeout.ms=45s` (default 10s) so a slow-starting consumer is not declared dead prematurely, and `heartbeat.interval.ms=15s` so heartbeats are not missed during long GC pauses. The architect's rule: use `CooperativeStickyAssignor` for any group with >5 consumers, do rolling deploys, and warm up consumers before joining — this reduces deploy-related stalls from 30 seconds to <1 second.
**Visual:**
```
eager rebalance (default pre-2.4): consumer joins -> pause ALL -> reassign -> resume
  -> 30s stall on every deploy with 12 consumers
fix 1: CooperativeStickyAssignor (KIP-429) -> only revoke partitions that move
  -> new consumer joins without pausing existing consumers
fix 2: static assignment -> stable across restarts
fix 3: rolling deploys (one consumer at a time) -> small rebalance per restart
fix 4: warm up before join (JVM, caches, downstream) -> ready immediately on join
fix 5: session.timeout=45s, heartbeat=15s -> no false deaths during slow start
result: deploy stall 30s -> <1s
```

### Q5. Your Kafka producer writes financial transactions with `acks=all` and `min.insync.replicas=2`. One broker crashes, dropping the ISR to 1 for several partitions, and producers start getting `NotEnoughReplicasException`. How do you handle this?
**Answer:** The diagnosis is that `min.insync.replicas=2` requires at least 2 in-sync replicas to acknowledge a write, but with one broker down (and `replication.factor=3`), some partitions have only 1 ISR (the leader), so writes are rejected — Kafka prefers to reject writes over accepting them with insufficient durability. The fixes, in order of safety. First, **fix the broker**: the priority is to bring the crashed broker back online — restart it, and it will catch up its followers and re-enter the ISR within minutes (depending on how far behind it is). This is the correct fix if the crash is transient. Second, **temporarily lower `min.insync.replicas` to 1**: if the broker cannot be recovered quickly, an operator can dynamically lower `min.insync.replicas` to 1 via `kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name <topic> --add-config min.insync.replicas=1`, accepting reduced durability (writes succeed with only the leader) until the broker recovers. This is a manual decision that should be logged and reversed as soon as the broker is back. Third, **provision for failure**: with `replication.factor=3` and `min.insync.replicas=2`, you tolerate one broker failure — but if a second fails, you lose availability. For higher availability, use `replication.factor=5` and `min.insync.replicas=3`, tolerating 2 failures. Fourth, **producer retry with backoff**: the producer's `retries` and `retry.backoff.ms` should be set high enough (e.g., `retries=Integer.MAX_VALUE`, `retry.backoff.ms=100ms`) so it retries through the outage instead of failing fast. The architect's rule: for financial data, use RF=3 + min.insync.replicas=2 + acks=all, accept that one broker failure causes brief write unavailability, and have a runbook for "lower min.insync.replicas if the broker cannot be recovered within 15 minutes." Stripe uses exactly this configuration.
**Visual:**
```
RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all
broker crashes -> some partitions have ISR=1 -> writes rejected (NotEnoughReplicas)
fix 1 (priority): restart crashed broker -> catches up -> re-enters ISR
fix 2 (manual): lower min.insync.replicas=1 -> writes succeed with reduced durability
  -> log decision, reverse when broker recovers
fix 3: provision RF=5 + min.insync=3 -> tolerate 2 failures (higher availability)
fix 4: producer retries=MAX, backoff=100ms -> retry through outage
runbook: 15-min recovery window, else lower min.insync
```

### Q6. Your Kafka consumer reads from a topic, processes each message (calls an external API taking 200ms), and commits the offset. The consumer is too slow — lag is growing. Adding more consumers does not help because all 12 partitions are already assigned. How do you scale?
**Answer:** The diagnosis is that the bottleneck is the external API call (200ms per message, synchronous), and the partition count (12) caps parallelism — you cannot add a 13th consumer because it would be idle. The fixes, in order of impact. First, **increase partition count** (the painful fix): re-partition the topic to 24 or 48 partitions, allowing 24 or 48 parallel consumers. This breaks key-based ordering (see Q3 in scenarios), so only do it if ordering is not critical or you can handle the split in the consumer. Second, **batch the API calls**: instead of calling the external API per message, batch 50 messages into a single API call (if the API supports batching), reducing the per-message latency from 200ms to 4ms — a 50x improvement without changing partition count. Third, **pipeline the API calls**: use an async HTTP client (e.g., `aiohttp`) to issue multiple API calls in flight per consumer, so a single consumer processes 10 messages in parallel — effectively 10x the throughput per partition without adding partitions. Fourth, **offload to a worker pool**: the consumer reads messages, enqueues them to an in-process thread pool (or a separate SQS queue), and commits the offset after enqueue (not after API call) — this decouples consumption from processing, allowing many parallel workers per partition. The trade-off is that an offset commit before processing means a crash loses in-flight messages (at-most-once on the API call); mitigate by committing after the worker processes, with idempotent API calls. Fifth, **use a different tool**: if the API call is inherently slow and per-message, Kafka may be the wrong abstraction — consider a queue with per-message ack (SQS) that scales consumers independently of partitions. The architect's rule: first batch and pipeline (cheap, 50x improvement); only then re-partition (expensive, breaks ordering); only then switch tools.
**Visual:**
```
12 partitions, 12 consumers, each does 200ms API call per msg -> 5 msgs/sec/consumer -> 60/sec total
lag growing, cannot add 13th consumer (idle)
fix 1: batch API calls (50 msgs/call) -> 4ms/msg -> 250/sec/consumer -> 3000/sec total
fix 2: pipeline async (10 in-flight per consumer) -> 10x throughput per partition
fix 3: re-partition to 48 -> 48 consumers (breaks key ordering)
fix 4: offload to worker pool (commit after enqueue) -> decouple consumption from API
fix 5: SQS (scales consumers independently of partitions) if API inherently slow
rule: batch + pipeline first (50x), re-partition last (breaks ordering)
```

### Q7. You need to replay the last 30 days of a Kafka topic through a new consumer to backfill a data warehouse. The topic has 100 partitions and 10TB of data. How do you do this without disrupting production consumers?
**Answer:** The replay reads from offset 0 (or from 30 days ago) on all 100 partitions, generating heavy read I/O on the brokers. The fixes to avoid disrupting production consumers. First, **use a separate consumer group**: the replay consumer is in its own group with its own offsets, so it does not interfere with production consumers' offsets. This is automatic in Kafka's design. Second, **throttle the replay**: set a per-consumer-group quota (`kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type groups --entity-name replay-group --add-config consumer_byte_rate=50000000` for 50MB/sec), limiting the replay's read rate so it does not saturate broker I/O. At 50MB/sec, 10TB takes ~56 hours — acceptable for a backfill. Third, **use follower fetching** (KIP-392): the replay consumer fetches from follower replicas, distributing read load across brokers instead of concentrating on leaders — this keeps leader-serving production consumers unaffected. Fourth, **run the replay during low-traffic windows**: if the topic has diurnal patterns (low traffic at night), schedule the replay to run faster at night (200MB/sec) and slower during the day (50MB/sec), using a dynamic quota. Fifth, **ensure retention covers the window**: verify `retention.ms >= 30d` before starting the replay, or the oldest data will be deleted mid-replay. Sixth, **checkpoint progress**: the replay consumer commits offsets periodically so it can resume after a crash without restarting from offset 0. Seventh, **parallelize**: run 100 consumer instances in the replay group (one per partition) to maximize parallelism within the throttle. The architect's rule: replays are normal in Kafka — design for them from day one by setting retention generously (30d+ for topics that may need replay), using follower fetching, and having a quota-based replay runbook. LinkedIn and Netflix run continuous backfill replays (new consumers reading from offset 0) without disrupting production, using exactly these techniques.
